lines.text: In nineteen ninety-six, id Software released Quake.
It changed how a generation saw three-dimensional space.
It went online. People rebuilt it, raced through it, and competed in it.
Underneath ran a monument of applied mathematics.
A software renderer: binary space partitions, a potentially visible set, a surface cache, fixed point.
Every pixel, one of two hundred and fifty-six colours.
And one division, rationed.
This is quake-srp: the slop rust port. Quake, ported to Rust by AI agents.
By default, it is the same renderer, given a twenty twenty-six machine.
Each departure from id is a named setting: a slop option.
Switch them all off, and you get Classic: id's game.
How do you prove a port is faithful?
Build id's own C to run without a screen: the oracle.
Give both the same camera, the same clock, the same monsters, and compare the frames, pixel by pixel.
Subtract one frame from the other, and this is what's left.
No, your video hasn't frozen. That's the difference: on these views, monsters and all, every pixel matches.
The mixer matches id's, sample for sample.
Demo playback matches frame by frame: the camera, every entity, every dynamic light.
One command runs ten checks, six of them against id's own C. All ten pass.
Now, the slop. We start from Classic, and switch it on one setting at a time.
First: torches.
id's mappers baked most of them into the walls, perfectly still: a hundred and forty-three, from the second map to the seventh.
The port finds each one with the light tool's own code, and lets it flicker, averaging to id's light.
The user asked for that: a warm feeling.
The lights id did animate are strings of letters, from a for dark to zee for bright, a new letter every tenth of a second.
On a sharp, fast screen they hold, then jump: a stutter in a smooth picture. Slop glides between the letters.
Monsters still think ten times a second. At two hundred and forty hertz, id's grunt stands still for twenty-three frames, then jumps.
Slop glides him, and blends his poses. Without the blend, he ice-skates.
id capped the game at seventy-two frames a second, and tuned it there.
Run id's code faster, and the physics drifts: at four hundred and eighty hertz, jumps peak higher, and grenades land further.
The slop preset draws a frame on every refresh, and steps gravity so that every jump lands on id's seventy-two hertz curve.
The clouds used to jump eight times a second. Now they drift.
Now, the picture.
Your screen's own pixels: square, and never smoothed.
id spread its ninety degrees across any width. On a wide screen, that cuts off the top and the bottom.
Horizontal plus keeps the height, and adds world at the sides.
The status bar scales up in whole pixels, and the brown strips beside it become more world.
QuakeC fires each nail six point seven units above the barrel. At ten-eighty, you can tell. So now they leave the barrels.
id's mixer runs at your device's rate now, with four of its bugs fixed. Like that click.
One last switch, and it's subtle.
id's renderer divided once every sixteen pixels, and drew straight lines in between.
Here is every divide.
The slop preset divides every eight pixels, as id's own portable C did. Why eight? Honestly, it felt right. A tenth more work, a quarter of the error: a good trade.
And that's the slop preset, switched on.
The rest is the same in both presets.
Every core draws its own bands of the frame. One thread or eight, the same pixels.
It runs in a browser, as WebAssembly.
It's fast, and it feels fast. Mouse-look, W A S D, a gamepad, a phone: even a zoomer can play it.
Claude, Anthropic's model, wrote the code, as fleets of agents, each on its own branch with a written brief.
A chair merged a branch only when every check passed.
The user set the rules: no dependencies, no unsafe code, and Classic proven.
Then played it, and said what was wrong.
id Software released Quake's source under a free licence. This port follows it, file by file.
Every change has a name. Every name can be switched off.
And underneath, pixel for pixel, it is still nineteen ninety-six.
